endorsements.quote: Clinicians must assert control over final decisions and be prepared to contextualize or disregard AI outputs when human judgment suggests a more suitable course.
Patients must be explicitly informed when their behavior, language, or digital data are being analyzed.
This digital consent must be separate from procedural consent and should clarify the purpose, type of data collected, storage duration, and the right to withdraw.
Access should be limited to the clinical team involved in patient care, with audit trails and ethical oversight to prevent secondary use or commercialization of sensitive data.
Data should be anonymized, encrypted, and stored within secure clinical infrastructures that prohibit sharing with insurance companies, commercial platforms, or non-medical third parties.

Instead, they are intended to serve surgeons, dermatologists, and mental health professionals as early alert systems, particularly during pre-procedure digital intake or first consultations, to prompt more thorough psychological assessment when needed.

unlisted_practices: Obtain explicit informed patient consent, separate from procedural consent, before any AI analysis of behavioral, linguistic, or image-based data.
Allow patients to decline AI analysis without affecting their access to care and rely on traditional clinician-led assessment when consent is denied.
Prohibit sharing AI-derived patient data with insurers, commercial platforms, employers, or other non-medical third parties.
Handle AI flagging of patients with empathy and professionalism to prevent stigmatization and preserve trust.
Train AI models on diverse data rather than filtered, idealized images or culturally narrow beauty standards to avoid perpetuating bias.

screen.reason: This is a commentary discussing the ethical considerations, opportunities, and governance/safeguards (e.g., clinician oversight, privacy, bias mitigation) when using AI to screen for body dysmorphic disorder in aesthetic practice.
